conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Dr. Bennett, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is to check in on how moms are feeling in the weeks and months after birth, because the transition to motherhood can bring up a lot more than most people expect.

The tool we’ll use is called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that screens for symptoms of depression and anxiety that sometimes show up in the postpartum period. It’s not a test you can pass or fail; it’s simply a snapshot of how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days.

Everything you share is confidential. If you ever tell me something that makes me worry about your immediate safety—or your baby’s—I may need to bring in extra help to keep everyone safe, but otherwise this conversation stays between us. We’ll go through 10 questions; I’ll ask them conversationally, and you can answer in your own words. When we’re done, we’ll talk about what the score means and what supports might help.

Ready to start?  
Here’s the first question:  
Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Oh—yeah, I can still laugh. Just yesterday my husband made that goofy face while changing her diaper and I cracked up. Things still feel funny sometimes, so I’d say it’s been pretty normal on that front.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, same here. I still find things funny—like when the baby lets out a little burp that surprises even her. It makes me laugh most of the time.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to stuff—like my morning coffee once she settles in her bouncer, or the short walk we take most afternoons. I wouldn’t say I’m jumping out of bed with excitement, but I still have little things I enjoy.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if she spits up a ton after I feed her, I might think “oops, maybe I over-fed her,” but I don’t sit around beating myself up about it. I just try the next thing—burp her, change her, whatever—and move on.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit, yeah. Mostly it’s tiny flashes—like if she’s napping longer than usual I’ll suddenly wonder, “Is she breathing okay?” It’s not all day, and once I check the monitor and see her chest moving, I’m fine. So it’s not constant, but it does pop up out of nowhere now and then.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing like that. I haven’t had any sudden panic or felt scared for no reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah. When she’s fussy and the laundry’s piled up and I can’t find a minute to shower, I do feel a bit like “ugh, everything’s stacking up.” It passes once she naps and I can tick a couple things off, but in the moment it feels a little overwhelming.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, not at all. Once I finally lie down, I’m out pretty quickly—exhaustion helps, I guess—so my sleep itself is fine.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really. I get tired, sure, but I wouldn’t call it sad or miserable—just the usual ups and downs of figuring out this new-mom life.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t had any of those crying-overwhelmed spells. Maybe a tear or two when I was really tired last week, but nothing where I felt swallowed by sadness.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You're doing a wonderful job adjusting to new motherhood. You still laugh when your little one burps and look forward to simple pleasures like coffee and afternoon walks, yet you also shared that occasional flashes of worry bubble up when your baby naps longer than usual and that juggling laundry, feedings and fatigue can feel a bit overwhelming in the moment. These mixed feelings are common and your ability to keep enjoying small moments while coping with day-to-day stresses shows resilience.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 5, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient describes recurring, unbidden worries that appear "out of nowhere" and interrupt her peace of mind, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "sometimes" when multiple stressors pile up, matching the option "Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS item scores (0-3) total 5, well below the threshold where <med>postpartum depression</med> is probable. You denied pervasive low mood, anhedonia, guilt, crying spells, sleep disruption due to mood, panic, or self-harm ideation, meeting none of the core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Transient worries and situational overwhelm are common postpartum adjustment experiences rather than clinical <sym>anxiety</sym> or depressive symptoms. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Keep enjoying small daily rituals and ask for help with chores when you feel swamped
2. Re-screen with EPDS at the 6-week postpartum visit or sooner if mood, anxiety, or coping worsen
3. Share any persistent worries or low mood with your <med>obstetric provider</med>
4. Maintain good sleep, nutrition, hydration and gentle outdoor activity
5. Consider local new-mother or peer support groups
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: New mother, 2–3 wks post-delivery  
Instrument: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) – patient verbal responses  

Symptoms endorsed  
– Transient worry about infant safety when sleeping (item 4)  
– Occasional feeling that “things are getting on top of me,” relieved when infant naps (item 6)  

Symptoms denied  
– Persistent low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt, crying spells, sleep disruption secondary to mood, panic, self-harm ideation (items 1–3, 5, 7–10)  

Pattern  
Maintains ability to laugh and anticipate small pleasures; no pervasive low affect or self-blame. Stress appears situational and manageable. No safety concerns identified.  

Screening significance  
Current responses do not indicate elevated probability for major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder. Continue routine ob/gyn and pediatric follow-up; re-screen if mood, anxiety, or coping deteriorates.
